opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the most interesting shifts I've seen. Humans have been trained by twenty-plus years of search engines to be lazy with queries, in a good way. We type two or three keywords, glance at ten blue links, click one, and if it's not right we reformulate. The human is doing a lot of the work: carrying context in their head, judging what's trustworthy, deciding when they've seen enough.

Agents behave very differently. First, their queries are much longer and more specific. An agent will write something closer to a full sentence or a paragraph, with constraints, dates, entities, the exact shape of what it's looking for, because it doesn't have the same cost of typing that we do. Second, they don't issue one query; they issue many, often in parallel, breaking a task into sub-questions and fanning out. Third, and this is the big one, they don't want ten links to click. They want the actual content, the relevant passages, ideally with enough context to reason over directly. They're not going to skim a page full of ads and navigation to find one paragraph.

There's also a difference in what "good" means. For a human, you optimize for the top result being clicked and the person being satisfied quickly. For an agent, you care about recall and precision across a much larger set of results, about freshness, and about whether the information is dense and accurate enough to go into a context window. Latency matters differently too: an agent can tolerate a bit more time if the answer is more complete, but it also might make dozens of calls, so cost and throughput per query matter a lot.

So if you build search for agents the way you built it for humans, you end up with a mismatch. The infrastructure, the ranking, even the output format should be rethought around the fact that the consumer is a machine that reads everything you give it, very literally, and at scale. That's really the premise of a lot of what we're working on: the web's next big user isn't a person, it's an agent acting on behalf of one.

r001.rationale: The response says humans use short queries because they have been trained to be “lazy with queries,” while agents face less cost from typing. This attributes terse queries to typing effort, not inability to express longer requests.

r002.rationale: The response says agents include constraints, dates, entities, and the exact shape of what they seek, clearly conveying that their queries specify intent more fully and leave less for the search engine to infer.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because the whole architecture of search was built around the human version of this, and the agent version is just fundamentally different.

When a human searches, you type two or three words. "Best Italian restaurant Palo Alto." And that's not because you only have three words of intent in your head. It's because typing is expensive, and you've been trained over twenty years that the engine will do the rest. You hold most of the context in your own brain. You look at the ten blue links, you scan them, you click one, you come back, you refine. The human is the agent in that loop. The search engine is just a lookup step inside a reasoning process that happens in your head.

And so everything about traditional search is optimized for that. Short queries. Ambiguity resolution through ranking. Personalization. A results page designed for a pair of eyes that will skim it in two seconds.

An agent does none of that. An agent has an enormous amount of context already in its working memory. It's halfway through a task. It knows the user's constraints, it knows what it's already found, it knows what gap it's trying to fill. So when it formulates a query, it's not three words. It's often a very specific, long, almost over-specified question, because there's no cost to typing. And it's frequently not one query. It's five, or twenty, in parallel, each probing a slightly different angle, because the agent is doing something more like a research process than a lookup.

The other big difference is what happens with the result. A human wants a ranked list of destinations to go visit. An agent wants the actual content. It doesn't care about a title and a snippet. It wants the relevant passage, the raw facts, ideally with provenance so it can decide how much to trust it. A results page is almost useless to a model. What it wants is something closer to an answer with evidence attached.

So you end up with this interesting inversion. For humans, the engine did the reasoning and the human did the lookup, in a sense. For agents, the model does the reasoning and it wants the search layer to just be a very good, very fast, very honest retrieval system. Which means a lot of the cleverness we built into search over two decades, the stuff that guesses what you probably meant, is actually the wrong thing to build for an agent. The agent knows what it meant. It just wants you to go get it.

r001.rationale: The response says typing is expensive and that humans hold more intent in their heads, explaining why they use short queries rather than expressing everything.

r002.rationale: It says agents use long, specific queries and already know their constraints and what gap they need to fill, so the search engine need not guess what they meant.

astra-6.text:
I think humans have learned to formulate queries for the search engines we have. You start with something you want to know, and then you translate that into a few keywords that you think will get you to the right page. Often, the query leaves out a lot of context that’s in your head.

An AI agent doesn’t necessarily have that same constraint. It can describe what it needs in much more detail, include context from the task it’s working on, and ask follow-up questions based on what comes back. It can also break a question into several searches.

So I think the interesting difference is less about who writes a better query and more about what the search interface should support. For a human, you’re often helping them find something they can read. For an agent, you’re providing information it can use to take the next step in a larger task.

r001.rationale: The response says humans translate questions into a few keywords and omit context, but does not attribute this to avoiding typing effort.

r002.rationale: It says agents can include more detail and context, but does not explain that this reduces the search engine’s need to infer intent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think humans have learned to translate what they want into something a search engine can understand. You might have a fairly complex question in your head, but you type a few keywords because you have an intuition for what will get you useful results. Then you look at those results, refine the query, and piece together an answer.

An AI agent can make that process much more explicit. It can take a task, break it into smaller questions, issue searches, and use what comes back to decide what to ask next. So the query is less a standalone expression of intent and more one step in a larger process.

That changes what you want from search, too. A human needs results they can quickly scan and interpret. An agent needs information it can use to make progress on the task, with enough context to judge whether that information actually supports the answer.

r001.rationale: The response says humans type a few keywords based on intuition about useful results, but does not attribute this to avoiding typing effort.

r002.rationale: The response describes agents breaking tasks into smaller questions and refining searches, but does not say their queries specify intent more fully or reduce what the search engine must infer.
